idiom_name: sealed state hierarchy + pattern-matching guards on distinct principals; enforcement in the service/policy layer
implementation_notes: Scala's realization is a closed state model plus pattern matching: a sealed trait or enum with case classes (Pending(initiatedBy), Approved(approvedBy)) and a match with a guard (case Pending(maker) if maker != currentPrincipal) makes every transition explicit, and the compiler checks that no state was forgotten when a new one is added. What is not in the language or the standard library is the enforcement point: the check must sit where the action is authorized - the application's policy/service layer, or a JVM framework such as Spring Security if the service is Spring-based - and the workflow row must move atomically (database transaction or lock) so two approvers cannot both observe Pending. Interop keeps the JVM's principal and security context available, but the distinctness predicate is yours to write and to test.
code_sketch:
sealed trait PaymentState
final case class Pending(initiatedBy: PrincipalId) extends PaymentState
final case class Approved(approvedBy: PrincipalId) extends PaymentState

def approve(p: Payment, who: PrincipalId): Either[Error, Payment] = p.state match
  case Pending(maker) if maker.value == who.value => Left(SelfApproval)
  case Pending(_)                                 => Right(p.copy(state = Approved(who)))
  case _                                          => Left(AlreadyDecided)
pitfalls: Pattern guards are runtime checks: if another path constructs Approved(who) directly (deserialization, a test helper, copy), the distinctness rule is bypassed.
Sealed hierarchies give exhaustiveness but not identity semantics; a distinct PrincipalId type (not a raw String) keeps argument-order mistakes from compiling.
On the JVM the acting identity often lives in a thread-local or security context; effect systems, thread pools and futures can lose it unless the principal is passed explicitly to the transition.
